title: Can Social Awareness Be the Secret to Thriving in Remote Tech Culture?
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni, a data analytics professional, argues that social awareness is the practical skill that lets people work well in remote and hybrid tech teams. She opens with a confession about interrupting a colleague on a wrong assumption, then offers four concrete practices: active listening to words rather than body language, noticing hidden cues of distraction on a video call, opening meetings with a personal win, and respecting colleagues' time off. Each is framed as a small, repeatable habit rather than a personality trait. The throughline is that reading the room and building rapport are leadership behaviors available to anyone on a team, and that they build trust, psychological safety and protection against burnout. The tone is conversational and experience-based rather than research-backed, but the advice is specific and usable.
points: Listening for words without bias, and checking your own assumptions before interrupting, is the base skill of social awareness in remote settings.
Visible disengagement on a call is a cue to stop and ask gently whether it is a good time, which signals care and often re-engages the person.
Opening recurring meetings with each person's win builds rapport and psychological safety at almost no cost.
Respecting off-hours (not expecting immediate replies, and saying so) prevents burnout and lets others set their own boundaries.
The author models fallibility by opening with her own mistake, which makes the advice credible.
quotes: I had an experience a couple of months ago when I interrupted someone in a large meeting, assuming they would ask me to do something misaligned with my project goals. The narrative in my head was, “Oh, great, one more thing I have to do!” They weren’t, and I had made a fool of myself.

Here’s how I tackle it so it rarely happens: In a remote environment, I mainly emphasize listening to the words vs. body language, as you can’t see everything as clearly when you are not in the same room. This is essentially a form of active listening. Being more present with your listening is a form of solid social awareness. An unconventional technique I have is focusing on the speaker's eyebrows. It’s less creepy than staring someone directly in the eyes, even in a remote meeting.

Is someone’s eye looking glazed over or focused on as if they see a ghost in the far left area of the screen? Has someone been off video the entire time and silent as a mouse? These are some hidden cues to know the unsaid from the meeting attendee, “I don’t want to be here!
Here’s what you do: ask gently if it is a good time for you to meet. You’d be surprised how often someone’s eyes shift directly on you, and they are suddenly all in.

Jumping right into business can backfire. With back-to-back meetings, people attending are not always focused. They are trying to pivot their brains after seeing the dumpster fire in their last meeting or being yelled at by a client. That’s cool - not. But here’s the thing—starting the call with someone unrelated who brings a spark of joy (a win) and sets the tone for the call. Most of all, it builds connections in a virtual world.
Taking time from the day to get to know people pays dividends later. It’s an easy routine to build into recurring weekly meetings. It builds rapport and psychological safety.

Allowing people to turn off helps prevent burnout. The line can get blurred significantly in the remote environment, where we reach each other through a DM or “quick question” through an impromptu meeting. People need a freaking break to thrive! You can set boundaries but also empower others to set boundaries, too.
